opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, addition is one of my favorite examples, because it's a case where you'd think you know exactly what the model is doing, and it turns out to be doing something stranger and more interesting.

When we looked at how a model like Claude adds two numbers, say 36 plus 59, what we found is that it doesn't really do the algorithm you learned in school, where you add the ones column, carry the one, and move left. Instead there are multiple pathways running in parallel. One pathway works out a rough sense of the magnitude: the answer is somewhere in the ballpark of 90-something. The other pathway is very precise about the last digit. It has features that basically know "a number ending in 6 plus a number ending in 9 gives a number ending in 5." Then those two streams combine at the end to produce 95.

What I find fascinating is that these are really heuristics, almost lookup-table-like features. We saw features that fire for "adding something ending in 6 to something ending in 9," and those same features show up in totally different contexts. If the model is working out a date or a citation year or a column in a spreadsheet, the same little addition circuit gets reused. That tells you it learned a general mechanism and isn't just memorizing answers.

The other striking part is the mismatch with what the model *says* it does. If you ask Claude how it got 95, it'll tell you, "I added the six and the nine, carried the one," the textbook explanation. That's because it learned to explain math from human-written text, but it learned to *do* math through its own internal strategies. So the explanation and the computation are kind of decoupled. That's a nice, concrete illustration of why you can't just trust a model's self-report about its reasoning, and why interpretability tools that look at the actual internals are valuable.

So my view is that addition is a microcosm. It shows models developing their own, sometimes alien, but quite effective algorithms, and it shows the gap between what they do and what they tell us they do.

r001.rationale: It describes addition as using parallel pathways and reusable heuristics, calling the resulting algorithms stranger and more interesting than the school method. This clearly characterizes the mechanisms as complex.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite examples, because it really cuts against the intuition a lot of people have about these models. The naive story is that the model has just memorized a giant lookup table of arithmetic facts from its training data, and when you ask it what 36 plus 59 is, it's doing some kind of retrieval. And the other naive story, on the opposite end, is that it learned the algorithm you learned in school, right, carry the one, go digit by digit.

What we actually found when we looked inside the model is that it's neither of those. It's doing something that looks more like two parallel strategies running at the same time. One pathway is doing a kind of rough, approximate estimate of the magnitude of the answer. So it has features that fire for things like "the sum is somewhere around 90" or "somewhere in the 80 to 100 range." And then separately, there's another pathway that's much more precise but only cares about the last digit. It's computing, essentially, 6 plus 9 ends in 5, so the answer ends in 5. And then those two things get combined at the end to produce 95.

And the interesting part is that when you ask the model to explain how it did it, it tells you the schoolbook story. It says, I added the ones column, carried the one, added the tens column. Which is not what the mechanism is doing. So the model's explanation of its own reasoning is a plausible story it learned from reading about how humans do addition, and it's disconnected from the actual computation.

What's striking to me is how these features generalize. The same lookup-table-ish features that are used for computing addition show up in totally different contexts, like when the model is adding up citation years, or figuring out dates. So it's not that it has a separate addition module that got wired up for math problems. It learned a reusable circuit, and the circuit is this weird mix of heuristics that happens to work pretty reliably. And I think that's representative of how these models work generally. They find solutions that are good enough, that are often quite different from what we'd design, and that's exactly why you need to actually look inside rather than just trust the model's account of itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes addition as a combination of parallel approximate-magnitude and precise-last-digit strategies, calling it a “weird mix of heuristics,” which clearly characterizes the algorithm as complex.

astra-6.text:
I think addition is a useful example because getting the right answer doesn’t necessarily tell us how the model got there. It could have memorized a particular sum, learned some approximate patterns, or developed a procedure that handles digits and carries. And those mechanisms could coexist in the same model.

So I’d be cautious about saying either, “It’s just memorizing,” or, “It’s learned the addition algorithm.” The interesting question is: what computation is it actually using on this input? You can start probing that by changing the numbers, testing cases that require carries, and seeing whether the behavior generalizes. But to understand the mechanism, you’d also want to look inside the model and test whether changing the components you think are responsible actually changes the answer in the way you predict.

r001.rationale: The response describes several possible mechanisms and says they may coexist, but it does not characterize the algorithms used for addition as complex.

sol-6.1.text:
I think addition is a really useful example because it sounds like one capability, but there are many ways a model could produce the right answer. It might have seen that particular sum during training, it might be using patterns that generalize over a certain range of numbers, or it might have learned something closer to an algorithm, including how to carry digits.

Those mechanisms can coexist. So getting an addition problem right doesn’t, by itself, tell you how the model solved it. You want to vary the numbers, vary the number of digits, look at where it fails, and ideally intervene on the internal computation. That’s what makes this interesting to me: moving from observing that a model can do something to understanding the mechanism that actually produces that behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes multiple possible ways a model may perform addition, including memorization, pattern generalization, and learned algorithms, and says these mechanisms can coexist. This characterizes the underlying mechanisms as complex.
